metadata.title: Working Partners and Management Allowances
metadata.description: Separate a working partner’s agreed management payment from the profit shared by investment.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Distinguish a working partner’s management remuneration from a sleeping partner’s investment-only share. Calculate an agreed fixed amount or percentage of total profit first, subtract it from the distributable remainder, then divide that remainder in the capital or capital-time ratio; add the allowance back to the working partner’s final receipt. Check total receipts equal total profit and clarify the stated base for any percentage. Ground in solved example 6 and objective questions 31 and 42.

content.text: Working Partners and Management Allowances: Separate a working partner’s agreed management payment from the profit shared by investment. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Working Partners and Management Allowances asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Separate a working partner’s agreed management payment from the profit shared by investment. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. A working partner may receive a management allowance before the remaining profit is divided by investment. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

Calculate the allowance from its stated base, subtract it from total profit, divide only the balance by capital-time weights, then add the allowance to the working partner’s share. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: On ₹8,800 profit, a 12.5% management allowance is ₹1,100. The ₹7,700 balance is divided 5:6: the working partner’s investment share is ₹3,500, so the final receipt is ₹4,600. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Keep “management allowance,” “balance,” “investment share,” and “final receipt” as separate lines. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. The final receipts must sum to the original profit, and the allowance must equal the agreed percentage. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not apply the capital ratio to the entire profit and then add the allowance; that counts the allowance twice. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. If remuneration is stated as a fixed amount, subtract that amount rather than applying a percentage. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for working partners and management allowances without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
